items.q: Where is our data stored and who can access it?
items.a: Access is governed by your workspace roles and permissions — you decide who sees what, down to confidential fields. Sign-in supports SSO via Microsoft Entra and two-factor authentication.

items.q: The AI reads our documents. Is that safe?
items.a: Darvis runs in Zero Data Retention mode: your company data is never stored by model providers or used for training. A human confirms key agent actions.

Freemium is free forever (tasks, document workflow, HR, dashboards, chats) — no credit card. Paid plans are a flat price per user per month: one subscription instead of 5–6 separate tools. Your counterparties always sign documents for free.

Cookies can be used to collect information generated by a website and stored via an Internet user's browser. A cookie is a small file or text information (usually smaller than one Kbyte) placed by a website on the hard disk of a user’s computer or mobile device via the user's browser. A cookie allows the website to temporarily or permanently “remember” the user's actions or preferences. Most web browsers support cookies, but users can set their browsers to reject cookies. Users can also delete the cookies at any time. Many users configure the cookie settings in their browsers to automatically delete cookies by default when the browser window is closed. Websites use cookies to identify users, remember their customers' preferences, and allow users to complete tasks without having to re-enter information when they move to another page or revisit the website later.

Cookies can also be used to collect information for targeted advertising and marketing based on online behaviour. For example, companies use cookies to track user behaviour and create personal profiles that allow them to show users advertisements tailored to their previous searches. There are different types of cookies. A classification can be made based on their lifetime:

items: Session Cookie: Session cookies are temporary cookies that are not permanently stored on the computer or mobile device used by the user. They are used as part of the login, authentication, and session management flows of the website. Certain session cookies are also used to understand, for example, if a user interacting with the website is a new visitor or a visitor returning as part of the same browsing session. These session cookies are erased when the user closes the browser, or after extended inactivity.

Persistent Cookie: Persistent cookies are those placed on the user’s computer or mobile device for a pre-determined length of time when a user visits a website. They are used on the website, for example, to understand (i.e. through Matomo services) what areas of the website are most popular, and how users engage with them.

blocks.html: Another classification can be made on the domain to which they belong:

items: First-Party Cookie: A First-Party Cookie is a Cookie stored on a user's device by the website they are currently visiting. These cookies are created and managed by the website's domain and are typically used to enhance user experience, remember preferences, and track user behaviour on that specific site.

Third-Party Cookie: A Third-Party Cookie is a Cookie which is created and managed by a domain other than the one the user is currently visiting. These cookies are often used for cross-site tracking, advertising, and analytics purposes, enabling businesses to understand user behaviour across multiple websites and deliver targeted ads based on those behaviours.

blocks.html: If the web server that feeds the website stores cookies on the user's computer or mobile device, these are referred to as “HTTP header cookies”. Furthermore, cookies can be stored by means of JavaScript code that is located or referenced on the page.

Example: A website is offered in five different language versions. When you call up the website for the first time, you select the language version “English”. A text file (a “persistent cookie”) including the information that you want to use the website in the English language is now stored on your device. If you do not delete the cookies and call up the website again with the same browser, the website will know from the stored cookie that the website is to be displayed in English.
More information on cookies can be found here: https://allaboutcookies.org.

sections.headline: Meet Your Future Workday.
sections.body: This is one working day, hour by hour, from the first notification to the last. Everything below already runs inside Darlean — the briefing, the meeting notes, the reports, the follow-up. Nothing here asks you to check a dashboard.

sections.headline: Every day begins with the same question.
sections.body: Most mornings start with reconstruction: opening the calendar, the inbox and three chats to work out what actually matters. That reconstruction is the expensive part, and it happens before any work gets done.

sections.headline: Darlean already has the answer.
sections.body: Darvis reads the day before you do and sends one message: how loaded the day is, what needs a decision, what can wait. You start from a conclusion instead of assembling one.

sections.headline: Your morning, in one screen.
sections.sub: Meetings, tasks and risks — laid out the moment you wake up.
sections.body: The briefing puts the whole day on one screen: how many hours meetings will take, which tasks you assigned and have not heard back on, and what needs your attention before lunch. It replaces the twenty minutes usually spent finding that out.

sections.headline: Walk into every meeting prepared.
sections.sub: Board meeting in 30 minutes. Last decisions, open actions and key risks — ready to review.
sections.body: Half an hour before a meeting, Darlean assembles what was decided last time, what was promised and what has not moved. Preparation stops being something you do at the last minute or skip.

sections.headline: Focus on decisions. We'll handle everything else.
sections.sub: Every discussion is transcribed, summarized and structured in real time.
sections.body: Nobody takes notes. The transcript, the summary and the list of what was agreed are built while the meeting runs, so the room can argue about the decision instead of about what was said.

sections.headline: Every meeting ends with execution. Nothing gets forgotten.
sections.sub: Minutes are generated automatically. Action items are assigned, deadlines are created and progress starts being tracked immediately.
sections.body: Agreements become assigned tasks with owners and dates before anyone leaves the call. The gap between deciding something and someone starting it closes to nothing.

sections.body: The afternoon is where the day usually slips: documents arrive, numbers need checking, and the decisions pile up behind them.

sections.headline: Every report, already reviewed.
sections.sub: Darlean reviews every incoming report, highlights material changes and prepares an executive summary before you open the document.
sections.body: The report arrives read. What changed, what it was driven by and what held steady are marked up before you open it, so the question becomes what to do about the numbers rather than what the numbers say.

sections.headline: A great day ends with nothing left to remember.
sections.body: The day closes itself: every meeting has a summary, every agreement has an owner, and nothing is waiting in your head to be written down later.
